title: AI Is Changing Military Morality
gist: Pope Leo XIV's encyclical calling just war theory 'outdated' actually smuggles in a revised version of it to govern autonomous weapons, requiring identifiable accountability chains and a 'moral timeframe' for lethal AI decisions — a framework the authors argue must be built out further as AI-mediated warfare increases the risks of escalation, weapons diffusion, and diffused responsibility ('dirty hands').

themes.theme: AI and autonomous weapons reshaping the ethics of war

insights.claim: As weapons become increasingly autonomous and AI displaces human decision-making in the military, wars can become easier to start and harder to control.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: A macro thesis on why AI-enabled warfare raises baseline geopolitical escalation risk, relevant for assessing defense-tech investment and conflict-probability models.
insights.quote: As weapons become increasingly autonomous and artificial intelligence displaces human decision-making, wars can become easier to start and harder to control.
insights.locator: That drone still required a human operator

insights.claim: The incorporation of AI into military capabilities on both sides of the Pacific adds layers between decision-makers and the killing, which can make resort to violence more likely even as weapons grow more precise, while also eroding accountability.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Suggests that improved weapon precision from AI does not reduce war risk and may increase it by lowering the perceived cost of engagement — a counterintuitive dynamic for those modeling great-power conflict probability.
insights.quote: the incorporation of artificial intelligence into military capabilities encourages a kind of warfare that creates additional layers between decision-makers and the killing. They can make the resort to violence more likely, even as it grows more precise.
insights.locator: On both sides of the Pacific

insights.claim: Autonomous weapons systems run on software, which can proliferate faster than any missile, magnifying the risk that weapons diffuse beyond the conflict for which they were built.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Flags software-based weapons proliferation as a faster-moving, harder-to-control risk category than physical arms transfers, relevant to export-control and non-proliferation policy.
insights.quote: Autonomous systems run on software, which can proliferate faster than any missile, magnifying the risk of diffusion.

insights.claim: Machine-based targeting creates a 'responsibility gap' where the law struggles to locate intent when a machine mediates the act of killing, inviting either unfair blanket liability for humans or the machine being used as an alibi for wrongdoing.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Identifies a legal and governance gap that defense contractors, militaries, and policymakers will need to resolve as autonomous weapons deploy at scale — a compliance and liability risk area.
insights.quote: When machines mediate the act, the law struggles to locate intent, inviting either an unfair standard that holds humans liable regardless, or the machine as an alibi for those who act badly.
insights.locator: For the use of autonomous weapons, the pope demands

insights.claim: The Pentagon's Responsible AI Strategy demands a traceable chain of accountability for autonomous weapons similar to the pope's encyclical, yet the same institution's emphasis on speed and efficiency in decision-making creates pressure that can deepen dependence on the machine and shrink the moral deliberation window.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: A direct tension within U.S. defense policy between stated accountability goals and operational incentives toward faster machine-driven decisions — worth monitoring for defense procurement and doctrine shifts.
insights.quote: the same Pentagon that requires traceable AI also prizes speed and efficiency—pressures that can deepen dependence on the machine, shrinking, if not displacing, that moral timeframe.
insights.locator: The pope also insists on a “moral timeframe”

themes.theme: The pope's encyclical on AI and warfare

insights.claim: Pope Leo XIV's first encyclical, 'Magnifica Humanitas: On Safeguarding the Human Person in the Time of Artificial Intelligence,' declared that just war theory 'has all too often been used to justify any kind of war' and is 'now outdated,' while also laying out ethical constraints for autonomous weapons.
insights.speaker: Pope Leo XIV (quoted by Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield)
insights.so_what: A major religious institution's formal position on AI warfare ethics that could influence policy debate, military ethics training, and public discourse globally.
insights.quote: it is important to reaffirm that the ‘just war’ theory, which has all too often been used to justify any kind of war, is now outdated.

insights.claim: The pope demands that autonomous weapons systems have an 'identifiable and verifiable' chain of responsibility running from designers and trainers of the system to those who authorize and employ it.
insights.speaker: Pope Leo XIV (quoted by Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield)
insights.so_what: Sets a normative benchmark that autonomous weapons developers and military buyers may increasingly be judged against, relevant to defense-tech compliance frameworks.
insights.quote: the pope demands a chain of responsibility that is “identifiable and verifiable,” running from those who design and train a system to those who authorize and employ it.
insights.locator: For the use of autonomous weapons

insights.claim: The pope insists that lethal-force decisions require a 'moral timeframe,' warning that 'speed and efficiency should never be the supreme motivating force for the irreversible decisions made in the context of war,' and that decisions must remain under 'effective, self-aware and responsible human control.'
insights.speaker: Pope Leo XIV (quoted by Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield)
insights.so_what: Provides a specific normative standard ('moral timeframe,' human control) that could be cited in future international AI weapons governance negotiations.
insights.quote: speed and efficiency should never be the supreme motivating force for the irreversible decisions made in the context of war
insights.locator: The pope also insists on a “moral timeframe”

insights.claim: The authors argue that despite challenging just war theory's relevance, the pope's own criteria for constraining autonomous weapons employ the tradition's same vocabulary and conditions, showing that no moral vocabulary exists to replace it wholesale.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: A meta-observation that even attempts to move beyond just war theory end up reconstructing it — suggesting any future AI-warfare governance framework will likely be an extension, not a replacement, of existing ethical/legal doctrine.
insights.quote: Confronted with the newest weapons in history, the encyclical could find no moral vocabulary but the tradition’s own.
insights.locator: The pope, in reckoning with these developments

insights.claim: The Vatican's doctrinal chief, Cardinal Víctor Manuel Fernández, argued at a summer consistory of 178 cardinals that just war theory now more often helps justify wars than prevent them, and the consistory reportedly considered replacing it with a narrower 'proportional defense' standard, but the authors argue this alternative offers little guidance to military planners.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Shows active internal debate within a globally influential institution over the future framework for judging the morality of war, with direct relevance to how AI weapons will be ethically evaluated going forward.
insights.quote: The consistory reportedly considered a narrower standard of “proportional defense” as a replacement, permitting self-defense in the strictest sense. But the proposed alternative answers only whether to fight, and only reactively.
insights.locator: Earlier this summer, Leo gathered 178 cardinals

insights.claim: The authors previously argued (seven years earlier) that proxy war introduces complications just war theory does not sufficiently address, based on the flawed assumption that if a proxy's cause is just, a benefactor's support for them is automatically just.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Establishes a template — proxy war ethics — that the authors extend to autonomous weapons, useful for understanding how legal and moral frameworks evolve to cover mediated forms of conflict.
insights.quote: Much of this comes from a single flawed assumption: that if a proxy’s cause is just, then a benefactor’s support for them is just.
insights.locator: Seven years ago in these pages

insights.claim: Providing a proxy with resources increases their incentive to escalate rather than resolve a conflict, and raises the risk of weapons diffusion, as seen when U.S. Stinger missiles supplied to Afghan fighters later surfaced in Bosnia and Kashmir.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: A concrete historical precedent for weapons-diffusion risk that the authors use to argue autonomous weapons software will diffuse even faster and more unpredictably.
insights.quote: Support for proxies also increases the risk of diffusion, that weapons migrate beyond the conflict they are provided for, as the Stinger missiles of Afghanistan later surfaced in Bosnia and Kashmir.
insights.locator: Support for proxies also increases the risk of diffusion

insights.claim: If a nation arms a proxy with advanced weapons without instituting practices to prevent indiscriminate use, that nation bears some responsibility for the proxy's resulting crimes — a dynamic scholars term the 'problem of dirty hands,' which the authors say directly parallels the accountability gap created by autonomous weapons.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pfaff, Patrick Granfield
insights.so_what: Extends an existing legal/ethical liability concept (dirty hands) from proxy warfare to autonomous weapons systems, a useful lens for anticipating future accountability litigation or diplomatic disputes.
insights.quote: if a nation provides a proxy with advanced weapons without instituting practices to prevent their indiscriminate use, then that nation bears some responsibility for their crimes, what scholars call the problem of dirty hands.
